turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack hesitated before explaining to Lady Bracknell that he was not certain how he had come to own a house in Belgrave Square, as he had been living in the country at the time.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen told her mother that she was tired of these tedious questions and that she was certain Jack was a perfectly respectable man.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell and Mr. Worthing that she would not stand for this sort of inquisition, and that she was perfectly well aware of Mr. Worthing's character and standing in society.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Mr. Worthing that his lack of clarity about his house in Belgrave Square was quite alarming, and that she could not possibly allow her daughter to marry a man about whom so many questions were being raised.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's expression turned stern as she asked Gwendolen to take her seat and be quiet, that this was no time for tantrums, and then turned back to Jack, her voice dripping with disdain, as she inquired about his family connections and social standing.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's incredulity was palpable as she asked Mr. Worthing to explain the circumstances surrounding his inheritance of a large sum of money.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell turned to Gwendolen, her voice stern, and told her that she would not be silenced, that her mother was merely trying to do what was best for her and that she should be grateful for her mother's efforts to protect her reputation.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell demanded to know the details of Mr. Worthing's education and upbringing, her voice firm and disapproving.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell expressed her dismay at Mr. Worthing's apparent lack of a respectable home in town, and insisted that he provide a satisfactory explanation for his living arrangements.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Mr. Worthing explained that he was raised by his late uncle, and that his education was largely self-taught, but he was proud to have acquired a good understanding of the world and its ways

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen called out to her mother through the carriage window, her voice firm and slightly impatient, telling Lady Bracknell that she was getting quite tired of being interrogated on her behalf.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Mr Worthing asked if it would be possible for him to provide some proof of his good character, such as a character reference or a letter from a clergyman, to put his mind at ease, and he hoped that this would be acceptable to Lady Bracknell.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen told her mother that she would not stand for such bullying and interrogations, and that she was beginning to think that Lady Bracknell was more interested in ruining her engagement than in getting to know her suitor.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen asked her mother to stop treating her like a child and to show some respect for her engagement

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he understood Lady Bracknell's concerns and was willing to answer any further questions she might have, in the hopes of putting her mind at ease about his suitability as a husband for her daughter

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he had been a ward of Chasuble's, the vicar, and asked if this might be considered some form of proof of his good character, and he was willing to have Chasuble vouch for his character if that would be acceptable to Lady Bracknell.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen said to Lady Bracknell and Jack that she would no longer be treated like a child and expected her mother to respect her engagement, and she would not be ignored any further.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen asked to be let down from the carriage, insisting that she would not remain hidden while her mother was interrogating her fiancé.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell and Jack that she would not be swayed by their questioning, and that her mind was made up regarding her engagement to Jack.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he was glad Gwendolen had intervened, and he hoped that her presence would help to clarify the situation and put an end to her mother's questioning.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell that she was engaged to Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Gwendolen and Mr. Worthing to pardon her, as they were not engaged to anyone. She explained that when they did become engaged, she or Mr. Worthing's father, if his health permitted, would inform them of the fact. An engagement should come as a surprise to a young girl, and it was hardly a matter she could arrange for herself. While she was making inquiries, Gwendolen would wait for her below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen called out to Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen to wait for her in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen replied to Lady Bracknell that she would wait for her.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Mr. Worthing to take a seat.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack stood tall, his eyes locked on Lady Bracknell, and said that he preferred to remain standing, rather than take a seat.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell informed Mr. Worthing that he was not on her list of eligible young men, although she had the same list as the Duchess of Bolton. However, she was willing to enter his name if his answers were satisfactory. She asked him if he smoked.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing admitted to Lady Bracknell that he smoked.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing smoked. She believed that a man should have an occupation. There were too many idle men in London. She asked Mr. Worthing how old he was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he was twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that twenty-nine was a good age to get married. She believed that a man who wanted to get married should know either everything or nothing. She asked Mr. Worthing which category he fell into.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that he knew nothing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing knew nothing. She believed that ignorance was a delicate and exotic fruit that should not be tampered with. She stated that education was unsound and produced no effect in England. If it did, it would be a danger to the upper classes. She asked Mr. Worthing about his income.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his income was between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing if his income came from land or investments.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that his income came from investments.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that Mr. Worthing's income was satisfactory. She stated that land was no longer a profit or pleasure, but rather a means of gaining position and losing it. She asked Mr. Worthing about his country house.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he had a country house with some land, but he did not depend on it for his income. In fact, the poachers were the only ones who made anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing how many bedrooms his country house had. She also asked if he had a town house, as a girl like Gwendolen could not be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he owned a house in Belgrave Square, but it was let by the year to Lady Bloxham.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing who Lady Bloxham was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack observed that Lady Bracknell went out very little, and that she was a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing what number his house in Belgrave Square was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his house was number 149.
